content.text: An image is a read-only stack of layers; a container is that stack plus one thin writable layer of its own. Everything the container writes, whether uploads, logs or a config file you fixed with
, lands in that writable layer. It survives restarts but is deleted with the container, and the image never changes. Data that must outlive a container belongs in a volume.
A small internal tool stores uploaded invoices under

inside its container. It runs for months without trouble. Then a routine deploy pulls the new image, removes the old container and starts a fresh one, and every uploaded invoice is gone. So is the timeout someone once fixed by running
and editing a config file. Nothing crashed and no command failed: the deploy did exactly what deploys do.
The belief: a container works like a virtual machine's disk. Whatever you change inside it is saved, into the container and from there into its image, so files written at runtime and fixes made with
It's easy to believe because it's half true. Stop a container and start it again, and your files are still there: in our test, a file written inside a container was still readable after
feels like SSH-ing into a server, and on a server, changes stay. Nothing in the day-to-day workflow warns you that the container you're editing is disposable.
The half that's missing: those changes belong to that one container. They never reach the image, and they disappear the moment the container is removed.
An image is a read-only stack of layers

Docker's docs state two principles. "Images are immutable. Once an image is created, it can't be modified. You can only make a new image or add changes on top of it." And: "Each layer represents a set of file system changes that add, remove, or modify files." A
is those layers stacked into one view of a filesystem. Running a container doesn't add to that stack.
A container adds one thin writable layer
When you create a container, Docker's storage docs say, "you add a new writable layer on top of the underlying layers." This

is where "all changes made to the running container, such as writing new files, modifying existing files, and deleting files" go. Image files are shared through copy-on-write: a container reads a file straight from the image layer, and the first time it modifies one, the file is copied into its writable layer and changed there. That's how many containers can share one image while each keeps its own changes.
Removing the container removes the layer
The same docs are blunt: "When the container is deleted, the writable layer is also deleted. The underlying image remains unchanged." Containers get deleted all the time: by
when they exit, and by every deploy that replaces an old container with a new one. In our test, a second container started from the same image found
empty while the first one still held the file. Stop and restart keep the layer; remove and recreate don't.

is the place for data that must last. The docs describe volumes as "persistent data stores for containers, created and managed by Docker", and say that "a volume's contents exist outside the lifecycle of a given container." Mount one at the path where your app writes, and removing the container leaves the data alone.
The fix: put data that matters in a volume
Here's the invoice tool's problem, reduced to Alpine and one file, on Docker 29.4:

tabs.label: ❌ Wrong
tabs.code:
docker run -d --name app alpine:3.22 sleep 3600
# bee75fd49ff55c594c6ac0e89c19f3f4725072fee5310dec0c332fef1cfedcee
docker exec app sh -c 'echo invoice-1042 > /srv/invoice.txt'
docker diff app    # what the writable layer holds
# C /srv
# A /srv/invoice.txt
docker rm -f app   # what a redeploy does to the old container
# app
docker run -d --name app alpine:3.22 sleep 3600
# 015ecf32f0e810a62b1bd0e13b6d9b0078c473f23c46ab2354656622f34e43d7
docker exec app cat /srv/invoice.txt
# cat: can't open '/srv/invoice.txt': No such file or directory

tabs.label: ✅ Right
tabs.code:
docker volume create invoices
# invoices
docker run -d --name app -v invoices:/srv alpine:3.22 sleep 3600
# 8d671a15136d29c25384471a3c014ca8712161f2c210faf688558a7f2b922a23
docker exec app sh -c 'echo invoice-1042 > /srv/invoice.txt'
docker rm -f app
# app
docker run -d --name app -v invoices:/srv alpine:3.22 sleep 3600
# 4a4d4c313774d830d3841a40f93001f61a7c0334e12fc6e7386c6d98a3565d4b
docker exec app cat /srv/invoice.txt
# invoice-1042

blocks.title: A fix made with docker exec dies with the container

content.text: Installing a package or editing a config file in a running container changes only its writable layer. The next deploy starts from the image again, without your fix.

blocks.title: A volume without a name is easy to lose

content.text: Volumes you don't name are anonymous. Docker's docs warn that if you start a container with
, "the anonymous volume associated with the container is destroyed" when it's removed. Name the volumes that hold data you care about.

items.title: Give lasting data a named volume

content.text: Mount a named volume at each path that must survive a redeploy, or move the data out of the container entirely, to a database or object storage.

In staging, remove the container and start a new one, then check that the data is still there. A restart can't catch this bug, because it keeps the writable layer.

items.text: An image is a read-only stack of layers; running a container never changes it.
Each container adds one thin writable layer, and every file it writes lands there.
That layer survives stop and restart, but it's deleted with the container, on every redeploy.
Data that must outlive a container goes in a named volume, outside the container's lifecycle.
